I love it. And you love it, too, because you've been working here for five years. Six years now? Okay. I'll talk first about the Academy School. Soon. The Academy School. The Academy School was founded in 1825, at a time when there were no art schools in New York. The founders, among whom were Asher Durand and Samuel Morse, thought that it was important for Americans to be given the chance to study in their own countries, own country rather than going abroad to London or Paris or Rome. So they began the school as a drawing society. Students would come with their pencils and paper, arrive at Samuel Morse's house. They would

share the expenses of light and models and work. The following year, in 1826, the system became more regular. They moved from one location to another, adding students and faculty. At the same time as the founding of the school, Samuel Morse began the academy itself, an association of artists. And one of the main obligations of the artists was to act every now and then as an instructor in the school. So some of the finest artists, painters, sculptors, printmakers in America in the 1820s, 30s, and 40s would give much of their time to the National Academy School. This system, this notion of responsibility on the part of the artist for the next generation of students, continued through this century, through the 1930s and 40s. the Academy School gained a reputation and was considered one of the finest art schools in America, an art school that followed the academic tradition, about which I'll speak more later. At the time that our friend Maurice Sievan studied at the art school, the system hadn't changed that drastically from the earliest system of the 1820s and 30s. Namely, the faculty was still drawn from the artist membership of the National Academy. These artists taught without pay. They gave their time in order to train the next generation. The tuition at the school was negligible. I remember a few months ago meeting a student from the 20s and 30s, actually from the Depression days, from the 30s, and he told me that he had received a scholarship to study at the National Academy School. I told him that I thought that the school was tuition-free. And he said, yes, the school was tuition-free, but there was a registration charge of $5, and there were special scholarships awarded to students who couldn't afford the $5 enrollment charge. The system that the school followed in those years was one that had been perfected among academies since their founding about 500 years ago in Bologna. Students would enter the school, they would present a portfolio, they would receive, they would present at the same time letters of recommendation from other artists or former students. They would begin copying from casts. This was, again, the traditional means of learning how to capture the human form. So a great deal of time was spent drawing from plaster casts. And once a certain proficiency was achieved, the instructor in the preliminary drawing class would then give the student the right to go into the life drawing class. So this is only on probation. And we have in our collection drawings done by students over the past 150 years, drawings of the live model, and stamped or written on the drawing would be the phrase, life on probation. In other words, the student was in the life drawing class, but only in a probationary way. And if he didn't maintain a certain degree of excellence, then he would go back to the drawing casts until the teacher thought that he was ready to make that important step. It's interesting, again, to look at some of these early drawings from students who had just moved to the live drawing class, because you can sense the difficulty that some students had in moving from the cast to the live model. The need to draw and the need to achieve a certain talent in capturing the human form is really the basis of the academic tradition. All the complexities, all the nuance of drawing is contained in the human figure, and to be able to capture it is the keystone, really, of our education. Students, once they developed a familiarity with drawing, would then paint or sculpt depending on the interest of the particular student. But it was the notion that drawing was the key, drawing was the crucial element that has been the focus of our school and other schools

like ours over the past 500 years. When Maurice was at the school, as I mentioned, this academic tradition had remained unabated. After the 40s, the tradition changed to a certain degree. The academy in the 40s and 50s no longer required this amount of practice with cast. And in the 50s and 60s, students could go directly into a life drawing class. Today, in 1985, this is certainly the case, we do offer the possibility to certain students, if they choose, to spend two or three weeks drawing from casts. But this is really just an exercise to teach certain aspects of drawing. We don't any longer feel that we can make that kind of a, a judgment that cast drawing is the important preliminary to drawing the model. And nor do I think that students today would have the patience the way they had in the early part of the century to spend that amount of time working from casts. So again, today we still do demand from our students experience in drawing, and students want that now. Students who 20 years ago might not have cared to learn about the figure now are coming to our school. They like the training, which is good. They like the idea that they can come to grips with this complicated human form of ours. We have instructors who are open-minded about how the human form can be represented. We aren't doctrinaire the way some people might have assumed years ago about our tradition. We are flexible in terms of approach, in terms of medium. We have people who are interested in abstract notions of the human figure who come and get the same kind of training that people who are more interested in the figure tradition also receive. (?)

My name is John Dobkin I'm the director of the National Academy of Design. I came to the Academy in 1978, not knowing a great deal about this place, though having worked only half a block away for the preceding seven years. The Academy, as I consisted of two parts: the school on 89th Street, existing in a 1950s building, and the academy itself, galleries, collection, living halfway around the block on 5th Avenue between 89th and 90th Streets. The school

architecture is interesting, it's kind of a mix, yet reflects or harkens back to a very important academy building, post-Civil War, built by Peter Bonnet White in 1864, a building modeled after the Doge's Palace. So passing along 89th Street toward Fifth Avenue on the right-hand side, halfway down the block, you see a rather severe facade with the brickwork suggesting in a certain fashion the Doge's Palace . At the same time, there's a small, there's a dose of 1930s I can't think of how I can describe it, but it's 1930s depression or 1930s Neo-Ailleurs . Rather forbidding, not very interesting, not very imaginative, not at all suggesting an art school. Modern, but not really. Dated, I'm sure, in the 1950s, a facade that's difficult to place, not one that captures one's eye. So we have this facade that doesn't tell us a great deal about our art school, a facade that I hope to adorn someday soon with banners and objects that are more appropriately part of an art school. (?) kind of art school. What can you tell us about, though, where the academy was in around the 20s? The academy was on Columbus Avenue and 109th Street in what had been considered temporary quarters, quarters that were built in 1909 after a very lengthy competition. The building occupied close to a city block and was in the area near the St. John the Divine. At the time the building was constructed, I think it was an interesting part of town, and the Academy at least thought it was. They wanted to be near Columbia, and as a matter of fact, at the time the building was constructed, there was some thought on the part of Columbia that the National Academy would serve as the fine arts component of the university. the academy became a bit nervous as smaller fish are of larger fish thought that they would be swelled by the university thought they would lose their identity and preferred to remain independent allowing Colombia to go off on its own to develop their own fine arts department but the school was was again in this part of town a part of town that became less and less attractive as the century wore on existing in a building that was never meant to last more than 20 years There were fires, there were leaks. It wasn't much fun. So in 1940, when an offer came from Archer Huntington, the owner of our present house, and his wife, Hannah Hyatt, the sculptor and member of the academy, in effect, to give the property to the academy, the members saw a way out. They saw a way out of an area that had been run down. They saw a way out of a building that really was pretty dreary. So the school that had rather spacious, if tattered, quarters in the first four decades of the century moved to 89th Street and 5th Avenue, out of the way at that point, and into a building that had been a house of the Huntingtons. There was no school, and the students who had numbered between 200 and 300 until that time were reduced to a much smaller amount, chiefly because the physical plant was so confining. The academy school, which certainly wasn't equal to and perhaps superior to the Art Students League in terms of quality and numbers until 1940, had to draw in its horns and move to 89th Street and to work out of one room, which I think had been the stable in the old house. The great pity was that the Academy, because of this reason, couldn't benefit from the enormous

boost in enrollment as a result of the GI Bill of Rights. The soldiers returning after the Second World War came to art schools as well as to other places, and these students couldn't be accommodated in the National Academy. This condition of working out of very modest quarters prevailed until the mid-1950s, when the Academy was able to raise enough funds to construct a building, the one that's presently in, on, 89th Street. Okay. Okay. Okay, my name is John Dobkin. I'm the director of the National Academy of Design. I've been at the Academy since 1978, thinking about its School of Fine Arts, about its exhibitions, programs, and collections. In the 1920s, the Academy lived on 109th Street and Amsterdam Avenue in a large, rambling building occupying almost a city block, a building that had been constructed in 1909 after a lengthy competition. The building was a halfway house. It was a temporary solution to a lack of space. The building was large, many studios. It was not well constructed. There were three or four fires, which destroyed some of the collection and some of the student work that had been housed in the building at that time. But it was immensely popular, very prestigious, difficult to get into, full of first-rate teachers and full of students who were determined to become artists. We've looked through photographs of the time in the 1920s, painting classes given by Leon Kroll, with three or four dozen students in very large, handsome studios, painting or drawing the model. People, some of whom are recognizable today, the Raphael Sawyers, Arshile Gorky's, Lee Krasner of the world, who were drawn to the school because it represented the very best and training of a time. That's it. Thank you.
